statement: In placebo-controlled laboratory and simulator studies of mostly healthy adults given a single dose of THC (80 studies, 155 trials, 3,454 participants, 71% men; McCartney et al., 2021; AMSTAR 2 critically low, provisional), THC compared with placebo is associated with impairment of most driving-related skills shortly after use, by small to medium amounts: lane weaving (standard deviation of lane position, Hedges' g -0.29, 95% CI -0.47 to -0.11), reaction time while driving (-0.47), tracking (-0.42), information processing (-0.38) and working memory (-0.36), among others, while driving speed was not worse (people tended to drive slightly slower). How long the impairment lasted depended on dose, route and how often people used cannabis. In people who used cannabis less than weekly, impairment grew with dose and faded with time, and, the authors say, may last longer after THC is eaten than after it is smoked or vaped: at the reference dose the authors modelled (amount in the study card), the average across skills was predicted to fall to the authors' chosen threshold of no meaningful impairment after about 5 hours when smoked, 6 when vaped and 8 when eaten, but information processing was predicted to take about 8 to 9 hours after inhaling, longer than the abstract's summary for cognitive skills says, and lane weaving, a driving measure, about 7 to 8 hours. People who used cannabis weekly or more were less impaired at the same dose, but their data were too uniform to model how long impairment lasts for them. These durations are predictions without confidence intervals from a model fitted mostly to tests within 4 hours of use; they assume steady recovery and say nothing about when any one person is safe to drive. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: In lab and driving-simulator studies, THC made people worse at driving skills such as staying in lane and reacting, by a small to medium amount. The effect faded over several hours: faster after smoking or vaping than after eating THC, and more slowly after bigger doses. People who use cannabis often were less affected, but nobody worked out how long it lasts for them. These are averages from a computer model, not a safe time to drive for any one person.
population: Mostly healthy adults (71% men) in placebo-controlled experimental studies published 2000 to 2020; duration models in people who used cannabis less than weekly
exposure: A single dose of THC, smoked, vaped or eaten, given by researchers (doses and timings are study conditions in the study card)
outcome: Driving performance in simulators or on the road, driving-related cognitive skills, and the predicted time for impairment to fall below a threshold
magnitude: Peak effects (Hedges' g, 95% CI): lane weaving -0.29 (-0.47 to -0.11); lateral control -0.24 (-0.41 to -0.08); driving reaction time -0.47 (-0.70 to -0.23); tracking -0.42 (-0.58 to -0.25); information processing -0.38 (-0.55 to -0.21); working memory -0.36 (-0.52 to -0.20); divided attention -0.28 (-0.36 to -0.20); speed +0.14 (-0.01 to +0.29). Regular use against other use in the combined inhaled model +0.17 (+0.06 to +0.28). Predicted recovery to g = -0.25 at the reference dose in other use: aggregate 300 min smoked, 350 min vaporised, 480 min oral; lane weaving 427 and 472 min; information processing 486 and 530 min (smoked, vaporised); no intervals given.

evidence.extracted: Peak effects shortly after THC (Hedges' g, 95% CI): divided attention -0.28 (-0.36 to -0.20), tracking -0.42 (-0.58 to -0.25), information processing -0.38 (-0.55 to -0.21), conflict control -0.34 (-0.42 to -0.25), reaction time -0.28 (-0.43 to -0.13), sustained attention -0.23 (-0.37 to -0.10), working memory -0.36 (-0.52 to -0.20); lateral control -0.24 (-0.41 to -0.08), lane weaving (SDLP) -0.29 (-0.47 to -0.11), driving reaction time -0.47 (-0.70 to -0.23); speed +0.14 (-0.01 to +0.29), not significant.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/McCartney_2021_THCImpairmentDurationMA.pdf (published version; minus signs checked on the rendered page)

evidence.extracted: Inhaled THC in other (mostly occasional) use, 481 effect estimates: impairment grew with dose (-0.0082 per mg, -0.0112 to -0.0053) and lessened with time (+0.0005 per min, +0.0004 to +0.0007), pseudo-R-squared 0.64. Combined inhaled model: regular use +0.1707 (+0.0572 to +0.2843, p = 0.003), less impairment, but pseudo-R-squared 0.0; regular-use model, no covariate significant, unsuitable for predicting duration. Oral model (243 estimates): impairment grew with dose with a U-shaped time course, pseudo-R-squared 0.28.

evidence.extracted: Predicted time for impairment to fall to g = -0.25 at the reference dose in other use, smoked / vaporised / oral, in minutes: aggregate 300 / 350 / 480; divided attention 383 / 428 / not calculable (oral peak predicted less impairing than g = -0.25); tracking 386 / 430 / 573; information processing 486 / 530 / 557; reaction time 232 / 276 / 492; working memory 277 / 321 / not calculable (oral peak predicted less impairing than g = -0.25); lane weaving (SDLP) 427 / 472 / not calculable; conflict control under 60 smoked, 71 vaporised and 665 oral; sustained attention under 60 inhaled. No intervals are given.
evidence.source_read: PDF PDFs/Cannabis/McCartney_2021_THCImpairmentDurationMA.pdf (published version; Table 9 checked on the rendered page)

evidence.locator: Abstract (p. 175); Table 9 and footnote b (p. 186); Discussion, paragraph on the inhaled model (p. 187, left column) and limitations (pp. 187-188)
evidence.extracted: The abstract says most driving-related cognitive skills would recover within about 5 h and almost all within about 7 h of inhaling the reference dose; in Table 9, information processing (486 and 530 min, smoked and vaporised) and lane weaving (SDLP, a driving measure: 427 and 472 min) take longer than 7 h. Limitations named by the authors: the models assume a fixed rate of recovery, few studies tested people who use cannabis regularly or longer intervals (4-6 h), doses were absolute rather than per body weight, and women were underrepresented. The recovery threshold (g = -0.25) is the authors' own definition of no meaningful impact.

risk_of_bias.note: Placebo-controlled trials of mixed quality (Rosendal mean 62%); review AMSTAR 2 critically low: unregistered, restricted search, no publication-bias assessment, primary-study quality not used in interpretation.

inconsistency.note: Large unexplained heterogeneity in the duration models (combined inhaled model pseudo-R-squared 0.0; regular-use model uninformative); predictions differ widely across skills.

indirectness.note: Worded for laboratory measures after single doses in occasional use, as studied.

imprecision.note: Predicted durations have no intervals and rest on few data beyond about 4 hours.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review; not downgraded separately.

grade.reasoning: Randomized placebo-controlled trials start high; risk of bias, inconsistency and imprecision each -1 give very low for the claim as worded, whose weakest necessary link is the predicted duration. The peak impairment estimates alone would rate higher (high minus risk of bias, moderate). Status replicated: many independent trials in the pooled analyses point the same way. The durations are model predictions for occasional use and are not presented as safe waiting times.
